active_trends.text: Removal of climate from security vehicles rather than only from language, and this week the pattern appeared in a bloc that has never been read this way. The Union published its largest climate-risk instrument to date — a proposed regulation with a mandatory warming trajectory, named risk owners and thirteen mandatory planning areas — and no defence or security institution appears in it anywhere. That is not removal; the referent was never placed in a Union security vehicle to begin with. So the trend now has three forms to distinguish: deletion from instruments that bind, demotion to premise in instruments that buy, and absence from instruments that were built in the civil-protection register and never had a security vehicle to be deleted from. The third is the Union's, and it is the hardest to reverse, because nothing was taken away and so nothing can be restored.

Closed this week, as last week said it should be, and replaced by the trend below. The finding it recorded held for ten weeks and is now complete: American adaptation survives federally only as emergency management, and the week's only federal act touching the hazard was a disaster declaration for Guam. What has displaced the reframing is no longer in doubt either — the institute's new programme line is artificial intelligence and its director has taken a seat in another country's government process. The question of where the capacity goes is a better question than the question of what it is called, so it gets its own trend. Closed in the week ending 2026-10-25 and retained for the record, because the finding it recorded held for ten weeks: American adaptation survives federally only as emergency management. One observation this week extends it rather than reopening it — India funds climate adaptation at scale through notified calamities and disaster response funds, with no climate-security vocabulary attached anywhere, which is the same structure arrived at by a different route and, unlike the American case, working. Successor trend: where displaced capacity goes.

Security Council shift from climate security to natural resource governance, and now past it. October closed on 30 October with the destination confirmed and one new data point that goes further than the trend predicted. The month carried no climate, water, food-security or environment item in any framing. On its last sitting day the Council held an open debate on maritime security built on artificial intelligence, autonomous systems and cyber capabilities — six weeks after the first United Nations declaration on sea-level rise, without touching it. So the narrowing is not confined to the resource agenda: where a subject the Council does discuss has an obvious climate dimension, the technological framing is taking the slot that the environmental framing might have had. The next test is elsewhere: the African Union's own Peace and Security Council has a climate, peace and security session on 11 November.

Retreat from binding multilateral environmental instruments — and this week, for the first time since the trend opened, movement in the opposite direction. The Union proposed a binding instrument whose core obligation is to plan against a stated warming path, and the science body whose certification every other instrument cites produced a date to try again: 1 to 3 December, virtually, with the assessment timetable and the budget both still open and several budget lines not agreed. Hold both at once. One bloc is adding a binding planning duty while the global certification machinery cannot agree when its next assessment arrives or how to pay for it, and the first will end up citing the second.

Dutch institutional creation with fiscal non-commitment, and this week the pattern acquired an external deadline and then had the pressure taken off it again. The Union's proposed law would require this country to designate a coordinating authority and name public authorities answerable for each major climate risk — the exact requirement a distributed governance model finds awkward — and the climate commissioner immediately devolved the choice of body to capitals, with the national deadline in June 2029. Meanwhile the 5 million euro structural defence line stands with its action plan four months overdue, no cabinet response on water at a seventh checkpoint, the parliamentary request for a single national briefing unanswered with eight weeks of the year left, and the final national adaptation strategy still promised rather than published. The pattern is now: a requirement exists, the deadline is distant, and the discretion is domestic.

The assets a changing hazard environment destroys are increasingly publicly indispensable, and this week the insurance side of the ledger acquired an official timetable and it is slow. The Union's answer to the protection gap is a Climate Insurance Alliance whose first measures are due by the end of 2027, which means there will be no independent public basis for estimating European catastrophe loss before 2028 and an insurer's proprietary model remains the only figure for the 2026 heat season. Against that, the week's two funds: almost two billion dollars approved for appraisable projects, and 20 million dollars set aside for one disaster. Indispensable assets are financeable before they break and barely compensable after.

The climate referent and the security register being decoupled by venue, and this week the decoupling was performed inside one institution in one document. The Commission's package carries the climate referent into a proposed regulation with a legal form and a reference warming path, and carries no security referent at all; the security word appears as the name of a planning area, water security, and in the title of a preparedness advisory group. Where the subject is risk the vocabulary is free; where the subject is capability it is absent; and where the subject is risk with legal force, the security register is simply not the register anyone reached for. That is the cleanest instance this trend has had, and it was produced by an institution that has no security instruments to protect.

The contest is moving from the hazard to the apparatus that measures and prices it, and this week the apparatus produced three things at once. A record: carbon dioxide at 426.8 parts per million in 2025, about 153 per cent of the 1750 baseline, published on the standing pre-conference slot. A reference frame fixed by law rather than by science: a proposed regulation making 1.5, 2 and 3 degrees the path every national risk assessment must use. And a certification body that has set a date to argue about its own timetable online in December. The apparatus is now being contested on three different axes — what the numbers are, who fixes the scenario, and who certifies the assessment — and this week each axis moved separately.

Forecast quality and institutional calendars have come apart, and this week the money moved for the first time since the trend opened. A 3.5 million dollar early-action allocation for Eritrea on 30 October, inside a programme described as up to 100 million dollars with more than 20 million already allocated across six countries — a figure that does not reconcile with the one this digest carried a fortnight ago, and no published breakdown separates anticipation from response. In the same week the peer-reviewed literature named the mismatch's components as findings rather than complaints: triggers too complex to use, protocols that diverge from practice, narrow evaluation, reliance on human judgement, uneven collaboration. The gap now has money crossing it, a research description of why it exists, and still no published lead time.

The evidentiary question for climate loss is shifting from attribution to foreseeability, and this week the question changed shape again. Until now the issue has been whether a measurable precursor obliges anyone. The Bhutanese outburst of 30 October shows that in a monitored basin with a national hydrology agency and a working cross-border notification habit, the precursor does not have to become a legal question at all, because the warning is issued and the loss does not occur. So there are now two futures for this trend. In basins with funded monitoring the foreseeability question dissolves into operations. In basins without it, the question hardens into liability, and the comparison to the funded basin next door becomes the claimant's best evidence. Which of the two a given valley gets is a budget decision taken years earlier, which is the trend's real subject.

Where displaced climate-security capacity goes. Opened a week ago with an answer — a foreign government's standing taskforce — and already needing a second one. The American institute whose director took that seat published its first climate research in a month on 29 October, and it is an assessment of European food security and climate resilience, written by a Europe-based visiting researcher, two days after the Union created a statutory planning duty. So the destination is not only a foreign public appointment; it is a foreign policy market, and the demand exists because that market has just legislated a reason to buy. This also corrects what this digest said three weeks ago: the institute's climate work did not stop, it changed customer. Three things to track now. Whether a second European-subject product follows. Whether any European institution cites the first. And whether the taskforce seat and the European publishing are the same strategy or two symptoms of the same vacancy at home.

open_threads.text: The Dutch institute's current funding phase. The route finally opened. After seven consecutive weeks of refused retrieval the platform's own site loaded this week, and what it shows is not a funding document but an answer to a different question: the platform states that it is powered by the Clingendael institute and gives a Dutch address, and every one of the seven items in its October news feed is somebody else's output — a Stockholm institute commentary on mine action and climate security posted on 28 October, an American institute's Gulf energy report, an Indian commentary, the Indian-Dutch South Asia report, a conflict-and-environment report, an alliance energy centre paper on radionuclides remobilised by wildfires and floods, and a peacebuilding film series. No funding information appears anywhere on the page. So the platform is a curation layer hosted by an institute, and the last publicly datable announcement of a funding phase remains December 2019. That is a stronger finding than seven refusals were, because the absence is now on a page that loads.

Whether the alliance published a fourth Climate Change and Security Impact Assessment. Still no, still no statement, and the displacing activity is now seventeen days silent. The alliance's climate centre has published nothing about its own Montréal summit of 15 and 16 October; its entire 2026 news stream remains two items, a spring course in May and a welcome to its fellows on 6 October, against published recaps of the 2024 edition on 30 October 2024 and the 2025 edition on 15 October 2025. Checked again this week. Two instruments, both opaque, and the comparator now makes it a contrast rather than a silence.

Whether the International Military Council's World Climate and Security Report has formally lapsed. Ninth consecutive week of silence. Its secretary general was on the Montréal speaker list and nothing has been published from that meeting either. One adjacent observable this week: the council's sister institute published a European food-security assessment, so the family is publishing again — just not this series and not in this register.
Funding trajectory of the joint United Nations climate security unit.
open_threads.resolution: Answered in magnitude, by a printed portfolio report rather than by the dashboard that has refused to render for three weeks. Cumulative deposits to the joint programme between 2016 and 2024 were $18.27 million, which places it thirteenth of fifteen funds in the trust fund office's climate and environment portfolio, against $808.89 million for the largest and about $2 million a year for this one. Fourteen governments contribute, eleven of them European; the Netherlands is not among them. The programme is not being wound down — a third phase runs 2026 to 2028 with ten advisers deployed — and it is funded at the level of a mid-sized national research grant. One consequence for this digest's own published record: Britain's £1 million of 25 September, reported here as three tenths of one per cent of a £331 million package and treated as a rounding error, is on the order of 5 per cent of everything this programme has ever received. The denominator was wrong. What remains unanswered is the year-by-year trajectory and whether the third phase has a stated requirement, which is carried forward as a separate question.

open_threads.text: Whether the 2028-2034 Union budget carries a security-tagged climate line. The external deadline fell and the answer is no, with the question displaced rather than closed. The resilience package carries no ring-fenced money at all; adaptation spending is to count towards the target of devoting 35 per cent of the next budget to climate and environmental objectives, which is a share of a negotiation rather than a line; an investment bank commitment of at least 30 billion euros across 2026 to 2030 is the only firm figure attached to it, and it is not security-tagged. No defence or security institution appears in the package. So the line does not exist in the instrument that was supposed to create it, and the only place left for it is the budget negotiation itself, where a policy debate is provisionally set for 11 December.

Chinese defence doctrine on climate. Eleventh week of nothing, and nothing dated inside this week from any Chinese venue. The positioning that carries over is the vice-minister's conference framing of 21 October — implementation, finance, the 300 billion dollar goal and its roadmap, and talks on the free flow of green technologies — which locates the climate problem in market access. The bilateral river mechanism with India produced nothing for a fifth week and its flood-season window has closed, so the next informative silence there is the dry-season exchange.

Any Indian security document on climate. Eleventh week of nothing, and this week supplies the strongest reason yet to think the question is mis-specified. India executed a six-figure pre-emptive evacuation against a cyclone on 28 October and has just enlarged the fiscal instrument that pays for such things — heatwaves and lightning added to the notified calamities for 2026-31, 2.04 lakh crore rupees recommended for state disaster funds across five years. The capability exists, is rehearsed and is funded; it simply has no security vocabulary attached to it anywhere. The three instruments that do carry the file stand: the treaty expiry on 12 December, the river mechanism with China, and the Delhi institute's argument about why South Asian climate cooperation does not happen. The committee route reconstituted on 26 September remains empty.
Swiss Re sigma citation for the $424bn 2025 protection gap.
open_threads.resolution: The citation is **sigma 1/2026**, *Natural catastrophes in 2025: the persistent rise of wildfire and storm risk*, Swiss Re Institute. The protection gap of $424 billion for 2025, up from $395 billion in 2024, with the natural catastrophe resilience index broadly stable at 27.3 per cent, comes from the Institute's Natural Catastrophe Insurance Resilience Index and is expressed in premium-equivalent terms. Caveat on strength: the reinsurer's own page would not open and the mirrored PDF's text could not be extracted, so the figures are corroborated across Swiss Re's own social post and several independent trade reports rather than read off the document.

open_threads.text: Whether any event attribution study of the 26 August Langtang-Lirung cascade appears.
open_threads.resolution: Resolved on 17 September 2026, and the answer is not one of the two the thread was framed to expect. World Weather Attribution published *Rapid Warming in the Himalaya Exacerbates Geohazard Cascades Beyond Adaptation Limits*, with contributors in ten countries across glaciology, mountain hydrology, climate science, seismology, humanitarian practice and social science. It attributes the hazard environment and not the event: about 1.5°C added to July-August temperatures by human-caused climate change, about 2°C annually — larger than global mean warming — individual winter months as much as 3°C, and the 0°C isotherm rising roughly 100 metres a decade into the bedrock that failed. It states explicitly that it has not assessed whether this specific rock-ice avalanche would have occurred without human-induced climate change, while asserting that warming at a rate beyond the global mean increases the likelihood and severity of such hazards. It then concludes that the event exceeded the design and predictive limits of existing risk reduction, that no existing early warning system could have provided sufficient lead time, that this constitutes a soft limit to adaptation given constrained habitable land and population increase, and that addressing loss and damage through recovery and reconstruction has become an unavoidable part of climate response. So: no event attribution, a hazard-environment attribution, and the policy conclusion reached through adaptation limits instead of causation. The successor question is the `adaptation-limits-adjudication` thread. Reporting figures that travelled with it: the debris flood ran 200 km in under seven hours at average speeds around 188 km/h and deposited 30.5 million cubic metres of material.

open_threads.text: What the HiRISK consortium is: membership, funding, institutional home.
open_threads.resolution: Resolved from hirisk.org, which was opened and read. HiRISK describes itself as 'a loose consortium of experts from High Mountain Asia and beyond', producing open risk datasets, dashboards, an expert database, risk assessments and peer-reviewed papers. Its listed member organisations include the Indian Institute of Technology Roorkee, the University of Central Asia in Tajikistan, a research group in Pakistan, a mountain-hazards institute in China, a hydrological institute in Bhutan, and two regional agencies including the Aga Khan Agency for Habitat. Stated support comes from Geo Mountains and from the Glacier and Permafrost Hazards in Mountains standing group of the International Association of Cryospheric Sciences and the International Permafrost Association. Funding amounts and sources are not disclosed, no individuals are named, and the site is labelled beta. Cite it as a consortium finding attributed to the consortium; do not upgrade it to institutional authority.

open_threads.text: What standard of evidence the loss and damage fund applies to a claim from an event with no event-level attribution. Unchanged, and the contrast sharpened this week by arithmetic. The other climate fund approved 1.97 billion dollars across 21 appraisable projects in four days, under published accreditation and review standards with stated review times; the loss and damage fund has set aside 20 million dollars for one disaster under no published evidentiary standard at all. The difference is not the money, it is that an appraisal regime exists on one side and does not on the other. The December board in the Philippines takes the long-term model, including rapid disbursement, plus the commissioned lessons assessment and the first project approvals.

Whether any part of the deltacommissaris's ask — 1 per cent of national output to at least 2 — survives into a government commitment. Seventh checkpoint passed in silence. No cabinet response, no figure, nothing dated inside this week from any Dutch water institution on the financing question, in a week when the chamber was sitting and when the Union proposed to oblige this country to name a public authority answerable for each major climate risk.

Whether an adaptation-limits argument is adjudicable by the institutions that will receive it. Unchanged on the adjudication and newly relevant on the planning side. A proposed Union regulation would require every member state to assess risk against a path reaching three degrees by the end of the century, which is the first time an adaptation-limits premise has been written into a legislative instrument rather than argued in front of one. That does not make the argument adjudicable, but it creates the administrative record an adjudication would later read: twenty-seven national risk assessments against a stated warming path, with named authorities attached to each risk.

Who bears the privately held share of Nepal's losses, and whether a sovereign loss and damage claim can cover them. Unchanged: nothing new from Kathmandu or the fund this week, the 20 million dollars still set aside against a 4.8 billion dollar recovery estimate, the proposal still the next document and the December board in Manila the next date. The week's comparator is worth recording against it: a climate fund that lends and appraises moved almost two billion dollars in four days, which is the route a hydropower operator's losses would actually have to travel if they were ever to be covered at all.

Whether any security institution reads the September sea-level declaration as a security instrument. The cleanest negative yet. On 29 October the Security Council held an open debate on maritime security and emerging technologies — artificial intelligence, autonomous systems, cyber capabilities — six weeks after the first United Nations declaration on sea-level rise, and took up neither the declaration nor statehood continuity nor maritime zones. A maritime-security debate that does not mention the sea level is the strongest available evidence that the declaration has not been received as a security instrument by the body it was aimed at.

Whether the alliance's removal of the climate referent from its binding resilience baseline is a drafting choice or standing practice. No new evidence, and the one piece that existed has not been corroborated in seventeen days: the centre of excellence that used the word freely on a programme page has still published nothing from the meeting where it used it. An adjacent finding arrived from outside the alliance this week — an American institute's assessment reports food security to be a fringe topic in dialogues between the Union and the alliance, including at the 2026 summit — which is a second instance of a hazard referent present in analysis and absent from the instruments.
Whether money reaches Somalia before the October-to-December rains.
open_threads.resolution: Answered yes, in part, and the answer required correcting this digest. Money did move before the rains: $7 million was pre-approved from the central emergency response fund in June for flood response preparedness ahead of the El Niño, alongside $10 million for drought response, and on 24 September Britain announced £5 million specifically for Deyr flood preparedness, split equally between a health, nutrition, water and protection programme led by Action Against Hunger and a Shabelle-basin rehabilitation programme delivered through three agencies, expected to reach about 600,000 people. Last week's digest said the money had not come; it had, one day before that was written. The proportions still carry the original finding: about £5 million and $7 million of anticipatory money against 2.5 to 3.5 million people exposed, roughly a million expected to be displaced, and a humanitarian plan at about a quarter funded. What happens next — whether the forecast verifies and whether the anticipatory money measurably reduced loss — is carried forward as a new question rather than as this one.

open_threads.text: Whether India or China responds to Nepal's proposal for a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism, made from the General Assembly rostrum on 24 September. Sixth week, nothing from either capital, and this week the proposal acquired a working demonstration elsewhere in the same range: a Bhutanese glacial lake outburst on 30 October produced warnings from Bhutan's hydrology and meteorology centre and advisories in West Bengal and Assam. A transboundary alert chain in the eastern Himalaya functioned while the central Himalayan proposal went unanswered. The mechanism Nepal asked for is not hypothetical; a version of it ran this week between two other states.

Whether the joint United Nations climate-security programme's third phase has a stated funding requirement, and whether contributions are rising, flat or falling. Unchanged and the route still not taken: the consolidated annual and financial reports for 2025 remain unopened. The unit's news stream has now been silent since 15 October. The denominator stands: everything deposited to it from 2016 to 2024 comes to 18.27 million dollars, which is less than a fifth of one per cent of what the main climate fund approved in a single board meeting this week.

Whether the climate panel remains the reference science for climate decisions, on what timetable, and which states are pressing on each axis. Sharpened by a date. The resumed plenary is called for 1 to 3 December, virtually, which is after the Antalya conference closes on 20 November — so delegations will open the second global stocktake without a certified assessment timetable. The positions are on the record from Addis Ababa: Saudi Arabia declining consensus on affected budget lines, India wanting the financial task team reconvened, Russia arguing the 2027 budget should be reconsidered if the work plan cannot be agreed, and the dispute itself turning on whether the three working group reports arrive in time for the 2028 stocktake or slip to 2029. The panel's own documentation warns the trust fund would be exhausted by the end of 2028 at 2025 contribution levels.

Whether any security institution treats the meteorological observing system's radio spectrum as an asset to be defended before the 2027 radiocommunication conference. Nothing again. One structural change worth noting against it: the Union's proposed resilience law would oblige member states to name a public authority responsible for each major climate risk, and an observing system is the dependency every one of those assessments will rest on without appearing in any of them. If a named risk owner anywhere identifies observational capacity as a risk to itself, that is where this question gets asked for the first time.

Whether any public institution produces an estimate of what Europe's 2026 heat season cost, to set against the private one. The deadline fell and the answer is no. The Commission published a public figure — about 200 billion euros of climate-related economic losses between 2022 and 2025, around 50 billion a year — which is a four-year aggregate and not a seasonal estimate, and the instrument that might have produced an independent basis for loss estimation, the Climate Insurance Alliance, is not due to deliver its first measures until the end of 2027. So the insurer's proprietary figure of about 113 billion euros of lost annual output across thirty countries is now the only number in circulation for the 2026 season, and will be for at least a year. That is the outcome this thread was opened to watch for, and it has happened.

Whether the Somali Deyr forecast verifies and whether the anticipatory money measurably reduced loss. The forecast continues to verify and the impact figures have started arriving. An October humanitarian update, relayed through press coverage rather than read at source, puts at least 175,000 people affected by El Niño-linked rains and flash floods across several regions, with the Shabelle rising towards moderate flood-risk thresholds at Belet Weyne and up to 3.4 million people in 44 flood-prone districts across 16 regions potentially exposed between October and December. Against the projection of 874,319 displaced and an appeal funded at 14.4 per cent, the first half of this thread is answered and the second is not: nobody has said who will measure whether the money reduced loss, and the week's foundational reading finds the evaluation of anticipatory action to rely on narrow metrics, which is the beginning of an explanation.

Whether any candidate for Secretary-General states a position on climate, and in particular on Council competence over it. Nothing new: no straw poll and no candidate statement found inside the week. The month closed with the Council failing to adopt either of two drafts on a peacekeeping mandate, which is the institutional condition any incoming Secretary-General inherits and the context against which an eventual climate statement would be read. The incumbent's term ends on 31 December.
Whether the climate panel's plenary at Addis Ababa, 12 to 16 October, decides the timetable for its next assessment, and on which side.
open_threads.resolution: Answered, and the answer is neither of the two sides. The plenary did not decide. On the evening of Friday 16 October the chair, Jim Skea, suspended the session after it had run past its scheduled close and after delegations from least developed countries and small island developing states had left, rather than put the question to the room; the panel's statement says the timelines for the three working-group contributions and the panel's budget both "remain open" and that deliberations will resume "at the earliest opportunity", with no date given. Both subsidiary questions are answered the same way: the review of the panel's own principles and procedures was deferred for a further session, and nothing was decided about the budget, which is the item with a hard deadline because the 2027 budget depends on it and the panel must reconvene before the end of the year to set one. This was the sixth consecutive session to fail on the timetable, and the last scheduled before the November conference opens the second global stocktake's information phase. Around thirty countries pressed for all three reports by about September 2028; China, India, Kenya, Russia and Saudi Arabia are reported on the side of delivery in 2029 for the impacts and mitigation reports. The thread closes because its question had a date and the date has passed. Its successor is ipcc-resumed-session-budget, because the live question is no longer which side wins but whether the body can convene to decide at all.

open_threads.text: Whether the Union's reported position that there is no scope for new climate finance commitments at the November conference survives into adopted conclusions, and whether it holds at Antalya.
open_threads.resolution: The first half is answered and the answer is yes in substance and no in wording, which is the more interesting outcome. Environment ministers adopted the conclusions on 12 October as document 14250/26. The reported phrase does not appear. What appears instead is an absence: no new figure, no new instrument, no new pledge, a cross-reference to the separate climate finance conclusions approved by finance ministers on 9 October, a restatement of the New Collective Quantified Goal and the global goal of at least US$300 billion a year by 2035, support for at least tripling adaptation finance by 2035, and the record that developed countries provided and mobilised US$132.8 billion in 2023 and US$136.7 billion in 2024. A position that commits nothing does not have to say so. The second question — whether the extension of the mitigation work programme to at least 2040 was what the line was traded for — is answered in the negative and this digest had it wrong: the word 2040 does not appear anywhere in the adopted text, which asks only for the programme to be continued and strengthened. What was actually traded away was international carbon credits, removed from the innovative-finance list amid member-state disagreement about their place in the emissions trading system; only carbon pricing survives. The thread closes here rather than at Antalya because the mandate is now fixed and the conference will test it rather than the question. One sentence from the same document outlives the thread and is carried into section B instead: paragraph 7 calls climate change an existential threat to humanity, ecosystems and biodiversity "as well as to peace and security".

open_threads.text: Whether the 1996 Ganges treaty is renewed, replaced or allowed to lapse, and on what terms. Forty-four days to expiry and the first date-stamped statement that no negotiation is under way: on 29 October Bangladesh said India had not responded to its request to negotiate a renewal. Dhaka's technical committee is headed by a prime-ministerial adviser, Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir; it wants a guarantee clause on dry-season flow and provisions covering climate change and the whole basin. India's position is that river matters belong in the Joint Rivers Commission, which this week's account independently places as last holding technical talks in May and last meeting at ministerial level in 2022 after a twelve-year gap. That supports the May date this publication's roster carried and leaves the meeting number unresolved; no number is now asserted. One load-bearing absence identified this week: no study apportioning Farakka dry-season decline between upstream abstraction and climate-driven hydrological change has been found, and a guarantee clause needs one.
Whether anyone publishes how much anticipatory climate money has actually disbursed, as against pledged.
open_threads.resolution: Resolved against this digest. The figure exists and has been public since 28 May 2026, in the fourth annual global overview of anticipatory action produced by the Anticipation Hub with the UN food and agriculture agency, the UN humanitarian coordination office, the humanitarian start network, the food programme, the German Red Cross, the international federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent societies, their climate centre and a German development agency. For 2025: anticipatory action triggered 146 times across 54 countries, almost US$120 million released, 9.6 million people directly reached, 262 active frameworks against 154 the year before, a further 205 frameworks in development across 71 countries, and 57 countries described as institutionalising the approach; Germany and the European Union named as the largest contributors among donors who supplied data; money for acting before a hazard reported separately from money for building the systems. Three caveats travel with it and none of them restores the thread: "released" is the report's own verb and is self-reported by the implementing organisations, there is no independent audit or counterfactual, and there is no breakdown of how far ahead of impact the money actually moved. That last is the successor question and it is now carried as anticipatory-lead-time-figure. For the record of what the figure means: almost US$120 million worldwide in a year is about US$12.50 per person reached, and roughly nine thousandths of one per cent of the US$1.3 trillion a year by 2035 that the November conference will argue about.

open_threads.text: Whether solar radiation modification's arrival in government climate-security forums is a one-off or the start of an agenda. Unchanged. Nothing from any government venue, and the institute that ran the Arctic tabletop published on European food security instead. Its director's seat on a national taskforce remains the place to watch, and that taskforce has still published nothing.

Whether the Pacific Islands Forum's own climate fund reaches its 500 million dollar initial capitalisation target by the end of 2026. Nothing new inside the week. Two months left. The comparison to keep next to it is this week's: a fund that has raised billions approved almost two billion dollars in four days because it has an appraisal regime, and a capitalisation total without a route remains a total.

Whether 1 million US dollars is the going rate for Dutch climate-security and climate-resilience money, or a floor the Netherlands happened to set at one venue. No new Dutch number. What arrived instead is a foreign institute's grading that places the Netherlands among four European leaders on food-security climate resilience, which costs nothing, is worth more reputationally than the pledge, and sits oddly beside a country with no published adaptation strategy and no named risk owner.

Whether the climate panel reconvenes before the end of 2026, what it decides about its 2027 budget, and whether the budget and the assessment timetable are taken together. The first part is answered: a secretariat letter of 26 October on the chair's behalf asks delegations to reserve 1 to 3 December, and the resumed session will be held virtually. The other two are open and the format now bears on them. Three days online, with the work plan and the budget in the same room, favours whichever decision can be taken without plenary debate, and the disagreement the suspension protected — states arguing for a timetable that allows meaningful participation and rigorous review — is the one least suited to a video link. The secretariat's estimate for completing the cycle is about 33 million Swiss francs; several 2027-2029 budget lines were left not agreed.

Whether the forty-eight-day precursor signal on the slope above the Gyirong-Rasuwa corridor is treated as foreseeability by any institution that has to decide something. No institution has, and this week supplied the operational counter-case that makes the omission harder to defend. In Bhutan on 30 October a monitored glacial lake emptied, the national hydrology agency issued warnings, and disaster authorities in two Indian states issued advisories. Monitoring, warning and cross-border notification all functioned in the eastern Himalaya in the same ten-week window in which a central Himalayan slope moved measurably for forty-eight days and nobody was told. The question is no longer whether foreseeability is technically available; it is why one basin's chain fires and another's does not, and what an obligor will make of that difference.

Whether anyone publishes how far ahead of impact anticipatory money actually moves. Still nobody, and this week both halves of the question got worse. On the money side, a 3.5 million dollar early-action allocation for Eritrea was announced on 30 October with no stated trigger, no stated threshold and no stated lead time, inside a programme described as up to 100 million dollars of which more than 20 million is said to be already allocated across six countries — a figure that does not reconcile with the more-than-50-million-for-eleven-countries figure this digest carried a fortnight ago, and no published breakdown separates anticipation from response. On the evidence side, the week's peer-reviewed synthesis of anticipatory action finds its evaluation to rely on narrow metrics, which suggests the number is not merely unpublished but uncollected.

Whether the first Dutch briefing on climate, nature and security is held during 2026, as a parliamentary motion asks. Eight weeks of the year left and nothing found. The comparison has moved on from the British taskforce: the Union has now proposed to oblige this country to designate a coordinating authority and name public authorities answerable for each major climate risk, with national assessments due by June 2029. A parliament that cannot obtain one briefing in eight months will be asked to legislate the owners of every national climate risk inside three years.

Whether the climate referent returns to a European Council conclusion in any substantive form. Not in a conclusion, and the institutional test returned a split answer. The Commission's package of 27 October carries the climate referent into an instrument with legal form and a reference warming path — far more than a conclusion would — and carries no security referent and no ring-fenced money. So the referent is back in Union law and still absent from Union security language, which is the decoupling this publication has been tracking, performed inside a single week by a single institution.

Whether the loss and damage fund's 20 million dollar ceiling for a single project and its out-of-cycle submission route become stated policy, and at what level. Unchanged this week, with the December board in Manila still the date. One new comparator from the same architecture: the main climate fund adopted an updated contributions policy for its third replenishment and its first policy for contributions from sources other than sovereign donors. If sovereign money is tightening enough for the large fund to write non-sovereign rules, the small fund's ceiling is unlikely to be raised by donors who have just been described as spending more on security.

Whether the projected tropical Pacific anomaly of up to 3.8°C for November to January verifies, and whether any security institution acts on the forecast before the peak. On the second question, six weeks and still nothing: no defence ministry, alliance body or security council has said anything about it, and the Security Council's two sitting days this week carried no climate item in any framing. On the first, the observed monthly anomaly is the datable answer and the peak is forecast for around December. What moved instead is humanitarian money — 3.5 million dollars of early action for Eritrea on 30 October — and impact: at least 175,000 people reported affected in Somalia in October.

Whether the British climate and nature security taskforce produces anything, by when, and whether any of it reaches a spending document. Nothing published, eleven days on from its first meeting, which is consistent with a body given up to two meetings in 2026 and no reporting date. This week's pushback bears directly on the test attached to this thread: the spending-document criterion is the right one for an advisory body and the wrong one for an instrument that sets a planning premise, and this is an advisory body. The criterion stands here.

Whether 'illegal exploitation of natural resources' becomes the Security Council's standing frame for resources and conflict. No reappearance in a Council product in the month's closing week, which carried a maritime security debate on emerging technologies and three mandate renewals. The next test is not at the Council: the African Union's own Peace and Security Council has a session titled on climate, peace and security in Africa scheduled for 11 November, following a postponed September session and a May meeting that tasked the Commission with mapping climate impacts in the Sahel and Lake Chad basin, with a common position on climate, peace and security possibly updated there. That is where the governance framing the Council declined would have to be restated.

Whether any government creates a body that is accountable for the gaps between its climate-security silos and gives it a budget line. The most consequential week this thread has had, and the answer is half of it. The Commission has proposed to require every member state to designate a central coordinating authority and to name one or more public authorities responsible for each major climate risk — accountability legislated — and the climate commissioner said explicitly that where that responsibility sits is for member states to decide, and attached no money. So the proposition that the problem is ownership rather than coordination has been adopted at Union level in its institutional half and declined in its fiscal half. What to watch is now specific and countable: which national body each capital names, and whether any of the twenty-seven names a defence, interior or security body rather than an environment or water ministry.

Whether the proposed European Climate Resilience Law reaches adoption with its two load-bearing provisions intact: the mandatory reference warming trajectory of 1.5°C by 2030, 2°C by 2050 and 3°C by the end of the century, and the duty on each member state to name one or more public authorities responsible for each major climate risk. Parliamentary treatment is reported as expected in 2027 and a Council policy debate is provisionally set for 11 December 2026. Three datable answers: whether the trajectory survives committee, whether the naming duty survives the Council, and whether any member state's eventual designation names a security, defence or interior body. The planning premise is the commitment here, not the money, which is this week's pushback.

Whether the African group's three requested agenda items — tripling adaptation finance, trade and climate change, and the main climate fund's financing arrangements — reach the provisional agenda and survive its adoption at the opening of the Antalya conference on 9 November. The mechanics give a clean answer within days: the secretariat may add items, parties adopt the agenda on the first day, any government may object, and contested items are diverted into presidency consultations. Watch also whether any other developing-country bloc backs the request at the pre-conference coordination meetings, and whether the trade item sinks the finance one by association.

How the Bhutan-to-India glacial-hazard alert of 30 October actually travelled, and whether anything equivalent exists on the Nepal-China border. The account that reports it working does not say whether the chain is a standing bilateral arrangement, a regional centre's relay or an informal call, and that mechanism is the asset. Three places an answer could appear: Bhutan's hydrology and meteorology centre, the Indian state disaster authorities that issued the advisories, and the mountain research centre's own follow-up assessment. Until one of them documents it, the field's best working example of transboundary early warning is undescribed.

Whether the environment programme's 2026 adaptation assessment was in fact published on 28 October, and if so why no launch, coverage or readable text can be found for it. The programme's own publication listing carries the date; its site would not open on any attempt, no press release was found, and no news coverage of the 2026 edition's contents exists. The emissions report of 21 October got a launch and set the numbers every delegation will quote at Antalya; the adaptation report, which is where the security-relevant finance gap lives, appears to have had none. Datable: whether the text becomes readable before the conference opens, and whether any delegation cites a 2026 figure from it.

Whether the finding that national governments, international organisations and the private sector are disengaging from climate and health is corroborated by any independent measure. It is the first cross-jurisdictional, multi-actor salience finding this publication has been able to cite that was not produced by a security institute, and it points the same way as this section's own readings for three of the six jurisdictions. Two routes to a check: the indicator series behind the claim, when the report becomes readable, and any comparable engagement index from outside the health literature.

open_moves.text: Denmark's Security Council food-security debate, outcome document unconfirmed. Closed as not produced. October has ended: the month's programme carried no food-security item in any framing, the only remaining route — the joint seminar with the African Union on 22 October — took illegal exploitation of natural resources instead, and the month closed on 30 October with three mandate renewals, two failed drafts on Western Sahara and an open debate on maritime security and emerging technologies. No outcome document traceable to the debate has ever appeared. A famine risk was classified in Somalia during the month and no Council member raised it.

open_moves.text: The American climate-security institute's philanthropic-funding bet. Fourth consecutive week of movement in the same direction and the register has now changed completely. The week's one new item is an event announcement for 27 October, "Charging Forward: Electric Vehicles as Defense Technology", moderated by the institute's own director, arguing that advanced batteries are a chokepoint technology on a par with semiconductors, that China dominates the supply chain, and that without a domestic electric-vehicle market the United States risks ceding a technology central to its future military capability. No climate content in the framing; no climate research published; a fourth week without a state-level briefer; the parent's new fellowship on artificial intelligence and national security closing applications on 20 October. This is a serious argument in the register that is currently funded, and it is not this field.

The Abyei climate, peace and security report and the next peacekeeping mandate renewal. Two findings this week, one of them a correction to this digest's method. The Stockholm institute's climate-change-and-security publications list still ends at the August Abyei study, checked again this week — but the institute published a commentary on integrating mine action into climate security on 6 October which does not appear on that list and surfaced only because another platform carried it on 28 October. So the list is not the institute's output and should not be read as a silence detector; that correction has been made to the standing roster. On the renewal: the mandates decided on 30 October were Colombia, the European force in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Libya, with two drafts on Western Sahara failing. None is Abyei, and no climate language was found in the three adopted texts as reported.
PIF security-declaration merger.

The Union's climate resilience framework, announced in the State of the Union address of 16 September. Delivered on 27 October, a day earlier than reporting of the pre-briefing had it, and the pre-briefing was substantially right: a hundred most-vulnerable territories to be identified, named risk owners to be designated by member states, a three-degree reference point for planning, and no ring-fenced money, with adaptation tied to the long-term budget negotiation. What the pre-briefing did not convey is the form — a proposed regulation with a mandatory reference warming trajectory and thirteen mandatory planning areas, water security among them — or the timetable, which runs to national plans by the end of 2030. Superseded by D2 on the ownership question and by the new thread on the law's passage.

open_moves.text: Succession to the Secretary-General. No seventh straw poll, no withdrawal and no new entry found inside the week. The month closed with the Council unable to adopt either of two drafts on a peacekeeping mandate, which is the institutional condition the choice is being made in. For this field the finding is unchanged through six polls: no candidate has been asked a public question about climate or about Council competence over it. The incumbent's term ends on 31 December.

The Turkish presidency of the Antalya conference, 9 to 20 November, with Australia running the negotiations. Advanced on the agenda rather than the substance: the African group has asked for three new items and the least-developed countries' lead negotiator calls adaptation finance a homeless issue, while China wants protectionism and green-technology flows addressed. The presidency's own action agenda carries an implementation bridge for turning national plans into investable projects. Two structural facts to carry into the meeting: the second global stocktake begins there, and the climate panel will not have a certified assessment timetable until December at the earliest.

Whether overshoot is adopted as a planning premise by security institutions or stays inside the climate-policy system. Advanced quietly and in the Union's own adopted text: the conclusions of 12 October reiterate the aim of "bringing the temperature increase to or below 1.5C by the end of the century", which is overshoot language adopted as a negotiating position without being described as such, drawing on the UN environment programme's report of 2 October. No security institution has adopted the premise, which is the original question and still unanswered.
open_moves.resolution: Completed, and promoted. What was a spotlight report on limiting overshoot on 2 September is now the headline of the programme's flagship pre-conference document: the Emissions Gap Report 2026, subtitled The Point of Return, treats exceeding 1.5°C as virtually unavoidable and reframes the objective as minimising the peak and the duration and returning below the limit by 2100. The move landed. What it did not carry with it is any treatment of adaptation, adaptation limits, loss and damage or security, in any of the published readings.

open_moves.text: The small island states' refusal of the overshoot frame. Still not restated: the group's most recent statement found remains 21 September, delivered by Anne Rasmussen at the conference action agenda launch, which calls for an urgent response to overshoot and for small island states not to be left out of the agenda's initiatives, and which mentions neither 1.5°C nor adaptation nor loss and damage. That is a different position from a refusal of the frame — it accepts overshoot as a condition and argues about inclusion. Either the refusal is being held for Antalya or it has been superseded by the week in which overshoot entered a proposed Union regulation as a planning path.

Whether the pre-event-indications finding produces a funded glacier-hazard early-warning programme, and whether it can survive the China-Nepal data wall. Advanced from an unexpected basin. The 30 October Bhutanese outburst shows the full chain working where the lake was already monitored — a 2015 event in the same headwaters had led Bhutanese authorities into glacial lake risk assessment work, and the centre reports permafrost monitoring with the same agency and flood forecasting across Bhutan, Nepal and Bangladesh under a development-bank-funded programme. So funded monitoring plus a national agency plus cross-border advisories exists in the eastern Himalaya today. Still no funding for the central Himalayan equivalent, and the bilateral mechanism that would carry a state-level data question remains silent.

Whether Nepal's restriction of foreign search-and-rescue becomes a precedent or an episode. Closed as an episode. Nothing has revived it in eight weeks, and Nepal's posture through that period has been outward-facing in every direction: a sovereign claim before the loss and damage fund, a regional mechanism proposed from the Assembly rostrum, and a joint cross-border scientific mission. The restriction was a decision taken in the first week of a disaster and not a doctrine.

open_moves.text: Whether the climate convention secretariat's economic-security framing is picked up outside the climate-policy system, and in particular whether any European security institution adopts the formulation.
open_moves.resolution: Answered on both halves and not in the way the question expected. A European security institution did adopt a security framing: on 24 September the Union's High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy co-hosted a foreign ministers' dialogue on climate change and ecosystem degradation as national security risks. But it adopted this field's own formulation, national security risk, not the secretariat's economic-security substitution. And the secretary himself substituted again in the same week, telling Climate Week that electrification shields countries, families and businesses from fossil-fuel supply shocks and calling it a development strategy, an industrial strategy, a health strategy and a security strategy — security fourth, and meaning supply security. So the two moved past each other: the institution reached for the field's register in the same week the secretariat reached past it. The question is closed because its premise has been falsified. It assumed the secretariat's phrasing would be the vector by which the security frame travelled into European institutions, and the frame travelled without it.

open_moves.text: Whether the deltacommissaris's two-per-cent ask converts into any government commitment. Sixth checkpoint passed in silence, and the external pressure arrived in a form that relieves rather than increases it. The Union's proposed law does require a named authority for each major climate risk, which is the awkward requirement for a distributed governance model — but the climate commissioner said where that responsibility sits is for member states to decide, and the national deadline is June 2029. A requirement with a devolved answer and a three-year clock is not pressure on this autumn's budget.

Nepal's claim on the loss and damage fund for the August cascade. Unchanged: 20 million dollars set aside on 22 October against a 4.8 billion dollar recovery estimate, plus 1.6 million dollars of oversight fees reported separately, nothing disbursed, no payment timeline, Nepal's own proposal the next document and the December board in Manila the next date.
Whether the rescission was announced as expected, whether the endangerment-finding proposal followed, and whether the Houston ministerial's outcome document mentions climate.
open_moves.resolution: All three answered. The partial repeal of the carbon pollution standards for fossil-fuel-fired power plants was finalised on 14 September 2026 by Administrator Lee Zeldin, signed at the G20 Energy Abundance Ministerial in Houston rather than on its sidelines; the agency prices it at $310 billion in savings and calls it the largest power-sector deregulatory action in US history. The separate proposal followed simultaneously: EPA proposed rescinding every remaining greenhouse-gas standard for the sector, the vehicle for repealing the power-plant endangerment finding, with $370 million in claimed direct compliance-cost savings. And the ministerial's outcome document, a Critical Minerals Meeting Communiqué, does not mention climate: it grounds critical minerals in energy security, digital infrastructure, emerging technologies and economic development, and calls for voluntary and collaborative cooperation respecting national sovereignty and 'different domestic pathways'. Canada's own readout of the meeting likewise contains no reference to climate change. Environmental organisations have said they will litigate. The substitution this digest read off the ministerial's branding last week is confirmed in a negotiated multilateral text, which is why this closes as landed rather than as too early.

open_moves.text: Whether the alliance ever states what happened to the Secretary-General's annual climate and security assessment. Still no statement, and the displacing event is now seventeen days unreported by either host. Checked the centre of excellence's own site this week: its most recent item remains the 6 October welcome to its fellows, and its whole 2026 stream is two items. Against published recaps of the 2024 edition on 30 October 2024 and the 2025 edition on 15 October 2025, plus a Canadian defence minister's speech for the 2025 edition, this is now a contrast and not a silence.

Whether the relocation of the evidentiary question from causation to adaptation limits is taken up by the institutions that have to apply it. Six weeks, and no fund board, bank, insurer or court has reasoned from adaptation limits. The premise has instead entered a legislative instrument from an entirely different direction: the Union's proposed law would require risk assessment against a path reaching three degrees, which is an adaptation-limits premise adopted administratively rather than adjudicatively. The attribution network published nothing on the Bhutanese outburst, the Horn of Africa or Europe's heat season this week.
Whether the American climate-security field's move to the state level is a durable relocation or a holding pattern.
open_moves.resolution: Answered no, and closed. Four consecutive weeks with no new state-level briefer since Ohio on 18 September; no state government named as commissioner or partner on any of the five; no second American institute writing for statehouses; and the institute's new programme capacity going elsewhere twice over — the parent's fellowship on artificial intelligence and national security, applications closing 20 October, and the institute's own event of 27 October on electric vehicles as defence technology. The statehouse series was one bet among several and it is not the one being pressed. The successor question is not where American climate-security work relocates geographically but which register it survives in, and on this month's evidence the answer is technology and supply-chain competition with China. That is carried by the csr-ccs-staffing move rather than as a new thread.

open_moves.text: Whether the asymmetry in the Dutch budget — flood defence funded, spatial adaptation and freshwater reduced over the longer term — survives the cabinet's response to the 2027 delta programme and the autumn estimates. No amendment and no cabinet response found; the parliamentary budget rounds on infrastructure and water fall later in the autumn, so this is still lead time. The defence line's action plan is now four months overdue. One new instrument on the same lane: the final national adaptation strategy and a new national implementation programme are promised before the end of the year, which is where the asymmetry would have to be either corrected or confirmed in writing.

The British, European and Kenyan foreign ministers' dialogue on climate change and ecosystem degradation as national security risks, 24 September. Five weeks on, no institutional follow-through from any of the three and nothing from the Union's external action service — which is now a sharper absence, because the Union published its largest climate-risk instrument this week and the service appears nowhere in it.

The British climate security package of September 2026. Unchanged: the taskforce has published nothing since its first meeting and the membership release of 21 October, and it has up to two meetings in 2026, no reporting date, no budget and no measurable target.

Nepal's proposal, from the General Assembly rostrum on 24 September, for a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism led by Nepal, India and China. Fifth week, no response from either capital, and this week a working comparator appeared in the eastern Himalaya: Bhutan's national agency warned and two Indian states advised, across a border, on 30 October. The unanswered proposal and the functioning chain are in the same mountain range and the difference between them is not technical.

The alliance's revision and first public release of its seven baseline requirements for resilience, 15 September. Nothing new from the alliance. The same operation — a hazard referent present in analysis, absent from instruments — was documented from outside this week, in an American institute's finding that food security is a fringe topic in dialogues between the Union and the alliance, including at the 2026 summit. And the Union's own new resilience instrument contains no security institution at all, which makes the pattern bloc-wide rather than alliance-specific.

Australia's Climate Week keynote on climate security as national security, 21 September, and the challenge to it from a former chief of defence asking where the plan is. Nothing new. Australia runs the negotiations at Antalya, where the agenda fight over adaptation finance will be the presidency's first procedural test, and the keynote and the chairmanship remain separate registers for the same minister.

Fiji's four-pillar position for the pre-conference talks, set out on 29 September. Nothing new inside the week. The regional declaration adopted on 6 October is the position that travels to Antalya, and the science pillar remains untransacted: the body it was aimed at will not have decided its own timetable until December, online.

The American climate-security institute's private tabletop on the security dynamics of a fictional 2030 stratospheric aerosol deployment, 14 October. No output and no participants named, as expected. What the institute published instead on 29 October was a European food-security assessment, which says something about the customer and nothing about the tabletop. Its conclusions remain the thing to watch for adoption.

Greece's Security Council programme of work for October, announced 1 October. Closed with the month. The finding held to the last day: no climate, water, food-security or environment item in any framing across the whole month. What the presidency ran instead was the succession, including the first colour-coded straw poll in the process's history on 16 October, a joint seminar with the African Union on 21 and 22 October that took illegal exploitation of natural resources, and a closing week of three mandate renewals, two failed drafts on Western Sahara and an open debate on maritime security and emerging technologies that did not mention sea-level rise.

What the presidency ran instead was the succession, including the first colour-coded straw poll in the process's history on 16 October, a joint seminar with the African Union on 21 and 22 October that took illegal exploitation of natural resources, and a closing week of three mandate renewals, two failed drafts on Western Sahara and an open debate on maritime security and emerging technologies that did not mention sea-level rise.

open_moves.text: The Berlin climate and security conference of 6 October, hosted by the German foreign ministry with the institute that founded it. Open on the only question the format leaves — whether any defence ministry repeats the weaponisation claim — and nothing this week repeated it. The alliance climate centre's note on the 2025 edition still has no 2026 equivalent, which remains consistent with a centre that publishes almost nothing.

The presidency's pricing of the climate finance ask against the alliance's defence commitment, made at the Nadi pre-conference talks on 8 October. The comparison has stopped being rhetorical. One European government has stated it will deliver only half of its 1.62 billion pound pledge to the main climate fund because it is spending more on security; two others have cut aid budgets; and the fund has responded by adopting its first policy for contributions from sources other than sovereign donors. The trade-off is now visible inside a treasury's arithmetic and inside a fund's resource-mobilisation architecture, which is where it counts, and in neither case has anyone argued it in public.
The Union's draft negotiating position for the November conference, reported on 6 October from a copy seen by a financial wire, stating there is no scope for new climate finance commitments.
open_moves.resolution: Landed, in substance and not in wording. The conclusions were adopted by environment ministers in Luxembourg on 12 October as document 14250/26 under the Irish presidency, chaired by climate minister Darragh O'Brien. The reported phrase is not in the text; what is in the text is an absence of any new commitment, a cross-reference to the separate climate finance conclusions of 9 October, and a restatement of existing goals. The expected trade did not happen: the word 2040 appears nowhere, and the mitigation work programme is only to be continued and strengthened. What was traded away was international carbon credits, deleted from the innovative-finance list; only carbon pricing survives. Two things from the same document outlive this move and are carried forward instead. Its paragraph 7 calls climate change an existential threat to humanity, ecosystems and biodiversity "as well as to peace and security". And its paragraph 11 condemns Russia's war of aggression and reiterates concern about the Middle East, in the strategic framing of a climate mandate, with nothing joining either to anything climatic — which is the current limit of what the Union will assert, in a text revised five times.

open_moves.text: The loss and damage fund's board called the first extraordinary meeting in its existence, for 22 October, on a draft decision provisionally setting aside US$20 million for Nepal and piloting a route for requests outside the fund's regular call for proposals.
open_moves.resolution: Held and decided. The board agreed unanimously to set aside 20 million dollars for Nepal plus 1.6 million in administrative and oversight fees — which settles last week's small question: the fees sit on top of the allocation, not inside it — and invited Nepal to submit a proposal for a later meeting. Nothing has been disbursed. The out-of-cycle route was used and then disowned as a precedent by three contributing governments; see D4. The decision text, by the only account that read it, says nothing about the standard of evidence a claim from an unattributed event must meet.

open_moves.text: The panel's chair suspended the sixty-fifth plenary on 16 October rather than decide without the delegations that had gone home. A secretariat letter of 26 October calls the session back for 1 to 3 December, virtually. The suspension has therefore produced a date but no resolution, and the format it produced is the thing to judge: see D4.

An Indian institute's workshop report with a Dutch partner, published 12 October, arguing that shared climate vulnerability in South Asia does not produce collective action because governance is national and siloed, sovereignty and information-sharing sensitivities constrain what can be proposed, and asymmetries make states facing one hazard set different priorities. This week gives it a hard test case: the alert chain that worked ran between Bhutan and India, two states with an asymmetric but unusually close relationship, while the proposal between Nepal, India and China remains unanswered. The report's own logic predicts exactly that pattern, which is a point in its favour and a reason to read it before designing anything regional.

The alliance's climate centre convened the Montréal climate security summit on 15 and 16 October, by invitation, on how to spend the climate-relevant share of a rising defence budget. Seventeen days on, neither host has published anything. Checked the centre's own site this week: its 2026 news stream is still two items. The thing to watch remains procurement metrics rather than communiqués, because climate-resilience metrics for defence procurement is the instrument that would let a treasury book resilience spending against both ledgers.

The Security Council's first use of colour-coded ballots in a straw poll on the succession, on 16 October. No seventh poll found inside the week. The only question that matters here is unchanged: whether anyone asks any candidate a public question about climate or about Council competence over it before the choice is made.

A British department published the membership of the first standing ministerial climate and nature security taskforce and held its inaugural meeting on 21 October. Nothing published since. Open until it publishes something or a recommendation of its appears in a spending document — and this week's pushback affirms that test for an advisory body of this kind, while withdrawing it as the general test of institutional seriousness.

The director of the Swedish peace research institute's climate programme argued on 22 October that climate security's problem is ownership rather than coordination, attacked the threat-multiplier formulation as naming no mechanism, and proposed one accountable central body with a budget line plus pre-agreed finance released on forecast thresholds. Five days later the Commission proposed to require every member state to name public authorities responsible for each major climate risk, with no money and with the choice of body devolved to capitals. The institutional half of the proposition has been adopted at Union level within a week of being put; the fiscal half has not. This is the fastest uptake of a research proposition this digest has recorded, and the causal claim is not being made — the instrument was in preparation for months.

The conference's president of negotiations named five ministerial pairs to facilitate mitigation, adaptation, finance, just transition and ocean, with no pair for loss and damage. The African group's request for a dedicated adaptation finance item is the first live test of whether that list is the whole architecture of the meeting or merely its opening position.

Germany, Czechia and Japan placed on the record that the fund's first allocation sets no precedent and is truly exceptional, against Pakistan's and Ecuador's attempts to make it learnable; the board did commission a lessons assessment. Unchanged until the December board in Manila. Worth noting that the three governments insisting on no precedent are among those whose aid and climate-finance budgets are under the security-spending pressure recorded elsewhere in these standing questions.

Ghana, chairing the African Group of Negotiators, wrote to the climate convention's executive secretary asking for three new Antalya agenda items — tripling adaptation finance, trade and climate change, and the main climate fund's financing arrangements. No other developing-country bloc had formally backed it at the time of writing. Open until the conference adopts its agenda on 9 November, which is a hard date.

Presenting the proposed Climate Resilience Law, the climate commissioner created a duty on member states to name one or more public authorities responsible for each major climate risk and said explicitly that where that responsibility sits is for member states to decide. Open until the Council and Parliament act and until capitals start naming bodies; the countable question is whether any of the twenty-seven names a security, defence or interior body.

The American climate-security institute published its first climate research in a month and the subject was European food security and climate resilience, by a Europe-based visiting researcher, two days after the Commission's package and engaging it directly. Open on whether a second European-subject product follows and whether any European institution cites this one.

A secretariat letter on the chair's behalf called the suspended sixty-fifth plenary back for 1 to 3 December, to be held virtually, with the assessment work plan and the trust fund budget as the only remaining items. Open until the session sits; the format is the part to judge, because three days online with the budget in the same room favours the decision that needs no debate.

The main climate fund's board adopted an updated contributions policy for its third replenishment and its first policy for contributions from sources other than sovereign donors, reappointing its executive director in the same meeting. Open until a contribution under the new policy is named and its source disclosed, which is the observable that would show whether the policy anticipates falling sovereign money or merely permits alternatives.
